    Top options

    The top 20 contracts (across this persona's portfolio) where the market's own implied volatility disagrees most with the volatility QuantLib priced them off — in volatility points, not raw dollar or percentage price gaps, which blow up meaninglessly for cheap, far-out-of-the-money contracts. Restricted to contracts within 12% of the money, priced at $0.50 or more, with a solved implied vol that's at least plausible next to the assumed vol (catches stale illiquid quotes); no ticker gets more than 3 rows, so one option chain can't crowd out the rest.

    How to read this. Three fixed portfolios — Conservative / Long-Term, Balanced / Core, and High-Risk / High-Reward — switchable with the tabs above; the same for every visitor, priced the same way. Balanced / Core is the actual weight-optimized output of the position_sizing.py risk engine; the other two are illustrative, equal-weighted starter lists. “Model” option prices are QuantLib's American finite-difference price, using each contract's own market-quoted volatility as input — it's a consistency check against the market, not an independent forecast. Each persona's options leaderboard ranks contracts by |model − market| as a percentage of market price and excludes any contract whose market price sits below its own intrinsic value — a real American option can never trade below intrinsic (you could buy and immediately exercise for a free profit), so a quote under that floor is stale, not a genuine mispricing. Those excluded contracts are tagged stale price in the contract tables below. See sigma_source in each contract table for where its volatility actually came from: a real market quote, a smile-interpolated estimate borrowed from the same stock's other quotes that day, or (last resort) the stock's own realized volatility. Dividends are priced as real discrete cash payments on their projected ex-dividend dates, sourced from each stock's actual payment history, with a graceful fallback to a flat continuous yield for stocks that lack a reliable schedule. The risk-free rate is a real short-end curve built from three live Treasury points (13-week, 5-year, 10-year), linearly interpolated, rather than a single flat number. This is still one flat volatility per contract, not a fully calibrated smile/surface model (e.g. Heston) — the smile-interpolation above is a practical stand-in, not a calibrated surface. The “since last check” badges next to each stock's spot price compare against the previous day's pricing run, refreshed automatically once a day. The price history chart in “Inspect one stock” is not backfilled — it starts recording the first day this dashboard tracked that stock and adds one point per day from there, so it grows a little more accurate each day rather than showing simulated history. Generated by price_options.py, append_price_history.py, and build_dashboard_multi.py from a live Yahoo Finance pull.
